questions.title: Configuring a Weekly Payment Process Request Template
questions.prompt: The client wants a recurring weekly payment run every Friday that pays all due US supplier invoices by check, excludes any supplier flagged on payment hold, and groups payments by supplier to minimize the number of checks issued. Walk through how you would configure this as a Payment Process Request template.
questions.modelAnswer: The consultant opens Manage Payment Process Request Templates, or creates a new template from the Submit Payment Process Request page and saves it. The selection criteria section is configured to filter invoices by business unit, US, due date through the processing date, and payment method or document type Check, ensuring invoices on payment hold are automatically excluded by leaving Include invoices on hold unchecked, relying on standard Payables hold validation already applied at invoice entry. The consultant sets Group payments by to Supplier, with Pay Alone set to No, so multiple invoices for the same supplier combine onto a single check, reducing check volume. The template specifies the payment process profile, linking to the correct bank account, check format, and document numbering sequence for the US disbursement account. The consultant sets up a schedule, either through Oracle's scheduled processes functionality with a weekly recurrence on Friday referencing the saved template, or documents the manual weekly submission procedure if automated scheduling isn't used. Before go-live, a test payment process request is run in a test environment to confirm the correct invoices are selected, holds are respected, and grouping produces consolidated checks as expected.
questions.professionalAnswer: I build this backwards from what the client actually complained about, too many checks, so grouping is the detail I nail down first. I set the grouping option so invoices for the same supplier combine onto one check rather than defaulting to pay-alone, which is usually what's driving the excess check volume in the first place. Then I layer in the selection criteria: US business unit, check as the payment method, and due date through the run date so I'm not sweeping up invoices that aren't due yet. For the hold exclusion I actually double check the template isn't set to include invoices on hold, because I've seen that checkbox accidentally left on from a previous template copy, and that's a compliance problem waiting to happen if a held invoice gets paid. For the Friday cadence I ask early whether they want this fully automated through a scheduled process or whether AP still wants a human to review the invoice selection report before releasing payment; a lot of clients actually want that manual checkpoint even if the selection criteria are automated, so I don't assume full automation just because it's technically possible. Before it goes live I always run it once against real test data, pull the preliminary selection report, and manually verify supplier by supplier that the grouping worked and nothing on hold slipped through.
commonMistakes: Leaves the template defaulted to pay-alone instead of grouping by supplier, defeating the goal of reducing check volume
Accidentally leaves include invoices on hold enabled, risking payment of a held invoice
Doesn't confirm whether the client wants full automation or a manual review checkpoint before release
Fails to link the correct bank account/payment process profile, risking payments from the wrong disbursement account
Skips a test run before go-live to confirm selection criteria and grouping behave as expected
keyPoints: Configures grouping by supplier (not pay-alone) to consolidate checks
Correctly sets selection criteria for BU, payment method, and due date
Confirms invoices on hold are excluded by default template settings
Links the correct bank account and payment process profile for US checks
Establishes scheduling (automated or manual-review) and validates with a test run before go-live

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly configures supplier-level grouping to reduce check volume
Correctly addresses hold exclusion and selection criteria
Addresses bank account/payment process profile linkage
Addresses scheduling approach and pre-go-live testing

questions.title: Fixing Intercompany Balancing Across Legal Entities
questions.prompt: Two legal entities share one primary ledger, and a recent intercompany transaction posted out of balance by legal entity even though the journal balanced at the ledger level overall. Walk through exactly how you would set up intercompany and balancing segment rules so this can't happen going forward.
questions.modelAnswer: The consultant first confirms that each legal entity sharing the ledger has a distinct primary balancing segment value assigned, since Oracle General Ledger requires balancing segment values to drive legal entity-level balancing, not just ledger-level. The root cause of the prior out-of-balance posting is typically a journal that debited one legal entity's balancing segment and credited another's without routing through intercompany accounts, which the system should prevent if balancing is properly configured. The consultant then configures or reviews Intercompany Balancing Rules, which specify the intercompany receivable and payable accounts used to automatically generate balancing lines whenever a journal would otherwise leave an individual balancing segment out of balance, even though the overall ledger balances. This involves navigating to Manage Intercompany Balancing Rules and defining rules at the ledger or legal entity level, specifying due-to and due-from accounts used to automatically balance by legal entity. The consultant tests this by entering a manual journal that crosses legal entities and confirming the system automatically inserts the intercompany balancing lines rather than allowing the journal to post out of balance by entity. Finally, the consultant reviews whether Balance by legal entity is correctly enabled on the ledger's accounting configuration, since this option must be active for the balancing rules to be enforced at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: When I hear balanced at the ledger level but out of balance by legal entity, my mind goes straight to one thing, balancing by legal entity probably isn't actually turned on for this ledger, or the balancing rules aren't catching this specific transaction type. So the first thing I check is the ledger's accounting configuration to confirm balance by legal entity is enabled, because without that switched on, the system has no reason to insert automatic balancing lines in the first place. Once that's confirmed, I go look at the Intercompany Balancing Rules setup and check whether due-to and due-from accounts are actually defined for the legal entity pair involved in that transaction; sometimes a client has rules defined for some entity pairs but missed adding a newer or less common pair. I also check whether each legal entity has its own distinct primary balancing segment value assigned, because if two entities somehow share one, the system literally can't tell them apart to balance between them. After fixing whatever gap I find, I don't just trust the configuration screen, I go simulate the exact scenario that broke, a manual journal crossing those two legal entities, and watch whether the system auto-inserts the intercompany due-to/due-from lines. If it does, I know the fix actually closes the gap rather than just looking right on paper.
commonMistakes: Doesn't check whether balance by legal entity is actually enabled on the ledger's accounting configuration
Assumes intercompany balancing rules exist for every legal entity pair without verifying the specific pair involved
Overlooks that two legal entities might be sharing the same primary balancing segment value
Fixes the configuration but doesn't retest with the exact cross-entity transaction scenario that caused the original issue
Confuses ledger-level balancing with legal-entity-level balancing
keyPoints: Confirms distinct primary balancing segment values are assigned per legal entity
Confirms balance by legal entity is enabled in the ledger's accounting configuration
Reviews/defines Intercompany Balancing Rules with due-to/due-from accounts for the relevant entity pairs
Understands the distinction between ledger-level balance and legal-entity-level balance
Retests using the exact cross-entity transaction scenario to confirm the fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the difference between ledger-level and legal-entity-level balancing
Correctly identifies balancing segment value assignment per legal entity as a root cause check
Correctly describes configuring/reviewing intercompany balancing rules with due-to/due-from accounts
Includes concrete retesting of the exact failure scenario

questions.title: Clearing Rejected AutoInvoice Lines in Receivables
questions.prompt: You run AutoInvoice to import 800 sales order lines into Receivables as invoices, and the output shows 740 succeeded and 60 rejected. Walk through exactly how you would investigate and clear those 60 rejected lines so they load correctly.
questions.modelAnswer: The consultant first reviews the AutoInvoice execution report, which lists each rejected line along with a specific error code and description, such as invalid customer bill-to site, invalid transaction type, missing or invalid line-level revenue account from AutoAccounting setup, invalid payment terms, or currency and UOM mismatches. Rather than guessing, the consultant queries the Receivables interface tables or uses the Transactions Open Interface workbench to see the actual rejected rows and their reject reasons grouped by error type, since similar errors are often systemic, such as one customer site newly added to source but not properly set up in Receivables, rather than 60 unrelated issues. For each error category, the consultant determines whether the fix belongs in the source data or in Receivables setup, such as adding a missing AutoAccounting rule, correcting a customer site's bill-to or ship-to association, or adding a missing payment term. Corrections are made at the appropriate layer, and the specific rejected lines are resubmitted by rerunning AutoInvoice scoped to just those corrected records rather than the full batch, to avoid reprocessing the 740 already-successful lines. After rerunning, the consultant confirms all 60 lines now show as successfully imported invoices in the Receivables Transactions workbench, and reconciles total invoice count and amount against the original 800-line source extract before closing the task.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I do is resist the temptation to just rerun the whole batch and hope it works better the second time; that wastes time and risks duplicating the 740 that already succeeded. Instead I go straight to the AutoInvoice execution report and actually read the specific error text for each of the 60 rejects, and I group them by error type rather than looking at them one by one, because in my experience 60 rejects is rarely 60 different problems, it's usually three or four root causes repeated. A classic one is a customer bill-to site that's new in the source system but hasn't been set up correctly in Receivables yet, and that alone can account for a big chunk of the rejects. Another common one is a missing AutoAccounting rule for a new transaction type or memo line, which throws an account-derivation error rather than something obviously about the customer. Once I've bucketed the errors, I fix each root cause at the right layer, sometimes that's a Receivables setup gap, sometimes it's genuinely bad data from the source extract. Then, critically, I resubmit AutoInvoice scoped only to the specific rejected lines sitting in the interface table, not the whole 800-line batch, and watch the output again to confirm all 60 clear. Only then do I do the final gut-check: total invoice count and dollar amount against the original source file.
commonMistakes: Reruns the entire batch instead of resubmitting only the rejected lines, risking duplicate invoices
Investigates rejects one at a time instead of grouping by error type to find systemic root causes
Fixes the symptom instead of the underlying setup gap, such as a missing AutoAccounting rule
Doesn't distinguish between source-data errors and Receivables configuration errors when deciding where to fix the issue
Skips the final reconciliation of total count/amount against the original source extract
keyPoints: Reviews the AutoInvoice execution report for specific per-line error codes/descriptions
Groups rejected lines by error type to identify systemic root causes
Correctly determines whether the fix belongs in source data or Receivables setup
Resubmits AutoInvoice scoped only to the corrected/rejected lines, not the full batch
Reconciles final invoice count and amount against the original source extract

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes investigating the execution report and error grouping
Correctly distinguishes source-data fixes from Receivables setup fixes
Describes scoped resubmission rather than reprocessing the full batch
Includes final reconciliation step

questions.title: Running a Full Cutover Rehearsal Before Go-Live
questions.prompt: You're two weeks from go-live and need to run a full cutover rehearsal for the Financials modules, simulating the actual go-live weekend end to end. Walk through exactly how you would plan and execute this rehearsal.
questions.modelAnswer: The consultant starts from the detailed cutover plan, a task list with owners, durations, and dependencies for each migration and freeze activity, and schedules a rehearsal that mirrors the real go-live weekend's timeline as closely as possible, typically run in a stabilization or pre-production environment refreshed to represent current production-like data. The rehearsal begins with simulating the legacy system freeze and final data extracts, suppliers, customers, open AP and AR balances, GL trial balance, open POs, timing each extract to validate it fits within the planned freeze window. Each FBDI load is executed in the same sequence as planned for go-live, with the consultant logging actual elapsed time for each step against the planned duration to identify bottlenecks. After loads complete, the team performs the planned reconciliation checks, total supplier count, open AP balance reconciled to legacy trial balance, GL opening balances reconciled by account, using the same validation scripts intended for the real cutover. Any failures are logged as defects with root cause and corrective action, and the cutover plan is updated based on rehearsal findings. The consultant also validates rollback and contingency procedures by confirming at what point in the sequence a go/no-go decision would need to be made if a step failed. The rehearsal concludes with a timing summary compared against the go-live weekend window and a go/no-go readiness report presented to the steering committee.
questions.professionalAnswer: I treat a cutover rehearsal as a dress rehearsal in the literal sense, same script, same order, same people, same clock, not a casual let's load some data and see. So I pull the actual cutover runbook and run it with a stopwatch, timing every single step against the planned duration, because the whole point is finding out now whether the real weekend has enough hours in it, not discovering that live. I always start by simulating the freeze and final extracts from legacy, because if those extracts take longer than planned, everything downstream shifts, and that's the kind of thing you want to know two weeks out, not two days out. As I run the FBDI loads in sequence, suppliers, customers, balances, open items, I'm watching for two things: did it load correctly, and did it take the time I budgeted. After loads finish I run the exact reconciliation checks we'll use for real, matching supplier counts, tying open AP to the legacy trial balance, tying GL opening balances, and I document every discrepancy as a real defect with an owner, not just a note to self. The part I think people underrate is defining go/no-go checkpoints during the rehearsal itself. I close it with a written timing summary against the go-live window and take it straight to the steering committee, because if the rehearsal doesn't comfortably fit inside the planned window, that's a conversation to have now.
commonMistakes: Runs the rehearsal informally without timing each step against the planned cutover window
Skips simulating the legacy freeze/extract phase and jumps straight to the Fusion-side loads
Doesn't run the same reconciliation checks planned for the real cutover, so gaps aren't caught until go-live
Fails to log rehearsal findings as formal defects/action items with owners and corrective actions
Doesn't define go/no-go decision checkpoints during the rehearsal itself
keyPoints: Follows the actual cutover runbook/task sequence, not an informal substitute
Times each step against the planned duration to validate the go-live window is realistic
Runs the same reconciliation/validation checks intended for the real cutover
Logs findings as formal defects with root cause, owner, and corrective action
Defines go/no-go checkpoints and reports a timing summary to the steering committee

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a realistic, sequence-accurate rehearsal mirroring the actual cutover plan
Addresses timing each step against the planned go-live window
Describes running real reconciliation checks during rehearsal
Addresses formal defect logging and go/no-go readiness reporting

questions.title: Configuring a Bank Account for Auto-Reconciliation
questions.prompt: The client's primary operating bank account needs to be set up in Oracle Fusion so that daily electronic bank statements can be loaded and automatically reconciled against AP payments and AR receipts. Walk through exactly how you would configure this end to end.
questions.modelAnswer: The consultant first ensures the legal entity and business unit structure is in place, then uses Manage Bank Accounts to define the bank if not already defined, the bank branch, and the specific bank account, entering account number, currency, and designating the account's use for payables disbursement and receivables receipts. The bank account is linked to the appropriate legal entity and assigned as the default disbursement account in the relevant Payment Process Profile, and as the receipt account for AR receipt methods. Under Cash Management, Bank Statement Transaction Codes are configured to map the bank's statement codes to internal transaction types, and Bank Statement Reconciliation Matching Rules are set up specifying matching criteria such as amount, date tolerance, and reference number for automatically matching statement lines to AP payments and AR receipts. The consultant configures the bank statement load process, typically via a BAI2 or SWIFT MT940 bank statement import template or a direct bank feed, to bring the daily electronic statement into the open interface, then runs Load Bank Statement and Autoreconciliation. Unreconciled items are reviewed in the Bank Statement Reconciliation UI, manually matched or researched if automated rules couldn't match them, and the account is reconciled with a confirmed ending balance matching the bank-reported balance, validated against the GL cash account balance as the closing check.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always build this in layers rather than trying to configure everything at once. First layer is just getting the bank, branch, and account itself defined correctly, and I pay close attention to currency and which legal entity owns the account, because getting that wrong means payments and receipts post from the wrong entity later. Second layer is linking the account into the actual transaction flows, making sure it's set as the disbursement account on the right Payment Process Profile for AP and as the receipt account on the AR receipt methods, because an account that exists but isn't wired into those profiles is just sitting there doing nothing. Third layer, and this is where the real reconciliation value comes from, is the matching rules; I set them up with realistic tolerances, usually a small date window and exact amount match to start, because too loose gives false matches and too tight means everything falls to manual review. For the statement feed, I confirm with the client's bank exactly what file format they're sending, BAI2 is still common, and I test the load process with a real sample statement file before go-live, not a fabricated one, because real bank files have quirks synthetic test data never shows you. After the first few automated reconciliation runs, I sit with treasury or AP and walk through every unreconciled item together, because that's really where you learn whether the matching rules need tuning.
commonMistakes: Sets up the bank account but doesn't link it to the correct Payment Process Profile or AR receipt method, so it's never actually used
Configures matching rule tolerances too loosely or too tightly
Tests the statement load with synthetic data instead of a real sample file from the client's bank
Doesn't confirm the correct legal entity ownership of the bank account before go-live
Skips the final reconciliation between the Cash Management reconciled balance and the GL cash account balance
keyPoints: Correctly defines bank, branch, and account with proper legal entity and currency
Links the account into AP disbursement and AR receipt methods
Configures bank statement transaction codes and matching rules with appropriate tolerances
Tests the statement load process with a real bank file format before go-live
Reconciles unmatched items manually and ties the final balance to the GL cash account

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes bank account setup and legal entity linkage
Correctly links the account into AP/AR transaction flows
Describes matching rule configuration with realistic tolerances
Addresses testing with real data and final GL reconciliation

questions.title: Executing a UAT Script and Logging a Defect
questions.prompt: You're executing a UAT test script for the 'Enter and Approve a Standard Supplier Invoice Over Approval Limit' scenario, and at step 6 the invoice routes to the wrong approver instead of escalating to the finance director. Walk through exactly how you would execute the rest of this test session and log the defect properly.
questions.modelAnswer: The consultant stops and documents the exact point of failure rather than skipping ahead, capturing the actual result at step 6, invoice routed to the direct manager, against the expected result defined in the test script, escalation to the finance director based on the approval limit rule, including a screenshot or export of the approval workflow history showing the actual routing. The consultant records the test environment, invoice number, amount, and user ID used, since reproducibility details are essential for the functional team to triage. Before abandoning the test case, the consultant determines whether downstream steps can still be executed independently using a workaround, or whether the defect blocks all subsequent steps, in which case those steps are marked blocked rather than failed or skipped in the test execution tracker. The defect is then logged in the project's defect management tool with severity and priority set to High, since incorrect approval routing is a control and compliance risk, a clear reproduction summary, expected versus actual result, environment, and a link back to the test script and step number. The consultant assigns the defect to the appropriate workstream lead, likely the approval rules configuration owner, and updates the overall UAT test execution summary to reflect the blocked or failed status, ensuring it's visible in daily UAT status reporting.
questions.professionalAnswer: The moment something doesn't match the expected result in a test script, I stop and document before I do anything else; I don't retest it three times hoping it was a fluke, because that just wastes time and muddies the evidence. I capture exactly what happened: the invoice number, the amount, who the approver actually was versus who it should have been, and I pull the approval history so whoever triages this can see the actual routing path rather than taking my word for it. Then I make a judgment call on the rest of the script, can I keep testing the parts that don't depend on correct routing, or does everything downstream genuinely depend on this step working? If it's genuinely blocked, I mark those steps blocked, not failed, because that distinction matters for metrics later. When I log the defect, I always write the expected result and actual result side by side in plain language, because vague defect descriptions are the number one reason things bounce back and forth between QA and the functional team without getting fixed. I set the severity high here because a payment approval control not working correctly is a compliance issue, not just a cosmetic bug, and I make sure it's visible in the daily UAT status so it doesn't quietly sit unassigned.
commonMistakes: Keeps retesting the same step repeatedly instead of documenting and moving on
Marks blocked downstream steps as failed or simply skips them without noting the blocking relationship
Logs a vague defect description without expected vs. actual result or reproduction details
Underestimates the severity/priority of an approval routing defect that has compliance implications
Doesn't capture supporting evidence, such as approval history, needed for triage
keyPoints: Documents expected vs. actual result with concrete details before moving on
Distinguishes blocked steps from failed/skipped steps in the test execution tracker
Logs a complete defect record with reproduction steps, environment, severity, and link to test script
Assigns appropriate severity/priority reflecting compliance/control risk
Ensures the defect and blocked test status are visible in UAT status reporting

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly documents expected vs actual result with reproducible detail
Correctly handles downstream blocked steps in the test script
Logs a complete, well-structured defect record
Assigns appropriate severity reflecting business/compliance risk

questions.title: Capitalizing Assets via the Mass Additions Process
questions.prompt: Fifteen capital invoice lines were coded to asset clearing accounts in Payables last month and now need to become fixed assets. Walk through exactly how you would run the Mass Additions process to capitalize them correctly.
questions.modelAnswer: The consultant first confirms the 15 invoice distribution lines were coded to an asset clearing or CIP account tied to a distribution set flagged for asset tracking, then runs Create Mass Additions from Payables, which extracts eligible capital invoice lines into the Mass Additions interface. In Fixed Assets, the consultant opens the Prepare Mass Additions workbench and reviews each of the 15 lines, which arrive with a status of NEW, verifying supplier, invoice, amount, and description information carried over correctly. For each line, the consultant assigns or confirms the asset category, depreciation book, units, and location, and determines whether lines should be posted as a single asset or merged if multiple invoice lines belong to one physical asset, using the Merge function to combine them before creating the asset. Lines are then changed from NEW to POST once ready. The consultant runs Post Mass Additions, which creates the actual asset records in the chosen depreciation book, moves posted lines to a POSTED status, and reflects the new assets in the Assets register with a cost basis, placed-in-service date, and depreciation method from the category defaults. After posting, the consultant checks the Mass Additions log for any exception-status lines due to missing category or invalid combination, corrects and reprocesses those, and finally verifies that Create Accounting for Assets generates journal entries relieving the clearing account and tying to the capitalized amount.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always double-check the source first; before I even run Create Mass Additions, I go back to the original 15 invoice lines in Payables and confirm they were actually coded to the asset clearing account and flagged with the right distribution set, because if that coding was wrong, nothing downstream fixes itself. Once I run Create Mass Additions and the lines land in the Prepare Mass Additions workbench with a NEW status, I go through them one at a time rather than batch-approving, because this is exactly where asset category and depreciation book assignments get rushed and wrong. One thing I watch for specifically is whether any of these 15 lines actually belong to the same physical asset, multiple invoice lines for one piece of equipment, say installation plus the equipment itself, and if so I use the merge function to combine them before posting, because capitalizing them as separate assets when they should be one is a cleanup headache later. Once everything looks right, I flip the status to POST and run Post Mass Additions, and then I immediately check for any exception-status lines rather than assuming everything posted cleanly, missing category or an invalid account combination are the usual culprits there. The step I never skip at the end is running Create Accounting for Assets and actually tracing that the clearing account got relieved by exactly the amount that moved into the new asset cost accounts, because that's the real proof the capitalization tied out correctly.
commonMistakes: Doesn't verify the original invoice distribution coding to the asset clearing account before running Mass Additions
Batch-approves lines in Prepare Mass Additions without reviewing category/depreciation book assignment per line
Fails to merge invoice lines that belong to the same physical asset, creating duplicate/fragmented asset records
Doesn't check for exception-status lines after Post Mass Additions and assumes everything posted
Skips confirming that Create Accounting for Assets properly relieves the clearing account against the new asset cost
keyPoints: Confirms source invoice coding to the asset clearing account before running Create Mass Additions
Reviews each line in Prepare Mass Additions for correct category, book, location, and units
Uses the merge function where multiple lines belong to one physical asset
Posts and checks for exception-status lines, correcting and reprocessing as needed
Validates Create Accounting for Assets properly relieves the clearing account against the new asset cost

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the Create Mass Additions to Prepare Mass Additions workflow
Addresses category/book assignment review and merge logic for multi-line assets
Addresses exception handling after posting
Addresses final accounting validation (clearing account relief)

questions.title: Auditing and Synchronizing Roles After a Reorg
questions.prompt: After a bulk reorganization, HR has updated supervisor hierarchies and several users changed job functions, but their Oracle Fusion role assignments weren't updated. Walk through exactly how you would run an access audit in the Security Console to find the mismatches and then synchronize roles for the affected users.
questions.modelAnswer: The consultant starts in the Security Console's Roles and Users areas, using role comparison and review features, and runs relevant security audit reports, such as a role provisioning report or OTBI-based security reports listing users by role or users whose role assignments haven't been touched since a given date. This output is cross-referenced against the HR-provided list of employees who changed job function or supervisor, identifying users whose currently assigned job or abstract roles no longer match their new position, for example a former AP clerk now in a GL role still holding an Accounts Payable duty role. For role-provisioning rules tied to HR attributes such as job code or department, the consultant checks whether those rules correctly fired after the HR update; often the real root cause is that autoprovisioning rules exist but didn't trigger because the HR change wasn't processed through the expected business process, requiring a manual Synchronize User Roles action in Security Console for affected users. For users without autoprovisioning tied to their change, the consultant manually revokes outdated roles and provisions the correct new roles via Manage User Role Assignments, sets appropriate effective dates, and documents each change for audit trail. Finally, the consultant reruns the audit report to confirm the mismatch list is empty and schedules a recurring periodic access review to catch future drift.
questions.professionalAnswer: My starting point is always the HR list, not the Oracle side; I take the actual list of who changed jobs or supervisors and treat that as my source of truth, then pull the role assignment data for exactly those people, because trying to audit the entire user population at once is how these reviews drag on forever and lose focus. In the Security Console I look at each affected user's currently provisioned roles against what their new job should have, and what I'm really looking for is whether this is an autoprovisioning problem or a manual-assignment problem, because the fix is completely different depending on which it is. If the client uses role-provisioning rules tied to job code or HR attributes, my first guess is that the HR update didn't actually trigger those rules, maybe it was done as a direct data correction rather than through the normal transaction, so I check whether running Synchronize User Roles against those specific users picks up the new job code and fixes it automatically. For anyone that doesn't resolve, I do it manually: revoke the stale role, provision the correct one, and I always note the reason and date in whatever change log the client uses, because six months from now someone's going to ask why a role changed and I don't remember isn't a great answer during an audit. Once I've cleared the list, I rerun the same report I started with to prove it's actually clean, and I usually recommend a recurring quarterly access review.
commonMistakes: Audits the entire user population instead of focusing on the specific HR-flagged list of changed users
Doesn't distinguish between an autoprovisioning failure versus a manual role assignment that was simply never updated
Manually fixes roles without checking whether Synchronize User Roles would have resolved it automatically
Fails to document the reason/date for each manual role change, creating an audit trail gap
Doesn't rerun the audit report afterward to confirm the mismatch list is actually cleared
keyPoints: Cross-references HR-provided change list against current Security Console role assignments
Distinguishes autoprovisioning failures from manual assignment gaps
Uses Synchronize User Roles where autoprovisioning should apply, manual revoke/provision otherwise
Documents each role change with reason and effective date for audit trail
Reruns the audit report to confirm the mismatch list is cleared and recommends periodic reviews

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly scopes the audit to the HR-flagged population rather than auditing everyone
Correctly distinguishes autoprovisioning vs manual assignment root causes
Describes correct remediation (synchronize vs manual revoke/provision) with documentation
Includes final verification/re-audit and recommends ongoing periodic review

questions.title: Recurring Invoice Stuck in Needs Revalidation
questions.prompt: A recurring non-PO invoice from a utility supplier has sat in 'Needs Revalidation' status for three days after the AP clerk edited the tax amount by hand to match the paper invoice. The automatically calculated tax line still differs from the manually entered line by $14.20, which exceeds the $10.00 line-level tolerance defined in the invoice tolerance template. The clerk insists the invoice total is correct and wants to know why validation keeps failing. Walk through how you'd diagnose and resolve this.
questions.modelAnswer: This is a tax setup and tolerance issue, not a data problem, and the first step is to separate the two. The candidate should open the invoice and compare the tax line Fusion Tax calculated against the amount the clerk hand-keyed: Fusion Tax calculates based on determinants in effect (supplier tax registration, transaction business category, tax rate code), while the clerk overwrote the amount to match the paper invoice without updating any determining factor. Validation reruns the engine's calculated value against the manual entry, and the $14.20 gap exceeds the $10.00 tolerance on the invoice tolerance template, so the invoice holds rather than failing outright. The diagnostic path is: (1) confirm whether the supplier's tax rate recently changed and Fusion Tax setup is stale, (2) determine whether the manual override reflects a legitimate rate change or a data-entry mistake, (3) confirm the $10.00 tolerance is the intended threshold for this supplier/category rather than an unreviewed default. If the tax rate configuration is wrong, correct the tax rule or rate so future invoices calculate correctly, then let the engine recalculate this invoice rather than keeping the override. If the manual amount is correct because the supplier applied a new rate early, update the tax rate's effective-dated record, not just this one invoice, and document the exception before resubmitting for validation.
questions.professionalAnswer: Tax variance holds like this are almost always one of two things: either the tax engine's rate is out of date, or someone typed over a line without realizing it breaks the automatic calculation. The first thing I'd check is the tax line detail on the invoice compared to what the clerk keyed in - I want the actual rate and determinants, not just the dollar difference. Nine times out of ten when a clerk says 'the invoice total is right, the system's wrong,' it turns out the supplier changed their tax rate or added a jurisdiction and nobody updated the tax rate setup, so the system is doing exactly what it was told. I'd check the supplier's tax registration and the effective dates on the rate record next. If the rate is stale, I fix it there, not on the invoice, because otherwise every future invoice from this supplier fails the same way. I'd also sanity-check the $10 tolerance with the AP manager - is that intentional for this category, or just a default nobody reviewed? Once I confirm the rate is correct, I'd reverse the manual override, let the engine recalculate, and only accept a manual tax line again with a documented, approved reason attached to the invoice so the next analyst isn't guessing.
commonMistakes: Raising the tolerance template limit just to make the hold disappear instead of finding out why the two amounts disagree.
Assuming the clerk's manual entry is correct simply because it matches the paper invoice, without checking the supplier's current tax rate setup.
Resubmitting the invoice for validation repeatedly without changing anything in hopes it clears on its own.
Fixing the tax amount on this one invoice without checking whether the stale rate will cause every future invoice from this supplier to fail the same way.
keyPoints: Recognize this as a tax-tolerance exception from a mismatch between Fusion Tax's calculated line and a manual override, not a system defect.
Review the tax line detail to identify the determinants (tax rate, registration, transaction business category) Fusion Tax used.
Check whether the supplier's tax rate or jurisdiction setup is out of date against the rate the paper invoice reflects.
Confirm the invoice tolerance template threshold is intentional for this supplier/category combination.
Correct the root configuration (tax rate record) rather than only patching the single invoice, and document any legitimate manual exception.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies root cause as a tax calculation/tolerance mismatch
Describes a logical diagnostic sequence across tax line detail, supplier tax setup, and tolerance template
Proposes a durable fix at the configuration level rather than only the single invoice
Addresses documentation or process change to prevent recurrence

questions.title: Same Supplier Paid Twice in One Week
questions.prompt: The AP manager discovers that a key IT services supplier received two payments totaling the same invoice amount within five days of each other, even though Fusion's duplicate invoice check is enabled. Investigation shows the invoices have different invoice numbers ('INV-4471' and 'INV-4471-A') but identical amount, date, and PO reference, and were entered against two different supplier sites that share the same remit-to bank account. Explain how you would trace the root cause and prevent recurrence.
questions.modelAnswer: The duplicate invoice check in Fusion keys primarily on supplier, invoice number, and amount combinations, and by default it will not catch two invoices with different invoice numbers even when amount, date, and PO reference are identical. The candidate should identify that the real exposure here is organizational, not a system bug: a second supplier site was set up for the same legal supplier and happened to share the first site's remit-to bank account, so the duplicate-number safeguard was trivially bypassed by appending '-A' to the invoice number. Diagnosis should trace the supplier site history (who created the second site, when, and why), confirm whether both sites were genuinely needed or whether one should be inactivated, and check whether invoice entry was manual versus a scanned/OCR import that introduced the suffix. Resolution has two parts: operationally, void or apply a credit against the duplicate payment, recover funds from the supplier if the payment was issued, and reconcile both invoices in the system. Structurally, consolidate to a single active supplier site where possible, enforce a review step before new supplier sites sharing a bank account go live, and consider enabling or tightening a PO-number-plus-amount duplicate check in addition to the invoice-number check so near-duplicate numbers on the same PO get flagged for manual review before payment.
questions.professionalAnswer: When a client tells me the duplicate check 'is on' but a duplicate still slipped through, my first move is to stop assuming the check is broken and instead look at what it actually compares. Fusion's duplicate check is really an invoice-number match, so a one-character difference like '-A' sails right past it - that's not a bug, that's a known limitation people forget about. So I'd pull both invoices side by side and confirm amount, date, and PO line match exactly, which tells me this was either genuine duplicate entry or two invoices for different partial amounts that happen to look alike. Here, the real red flag for me is the shared bank account across two supplier sites - that's a setup problem, and in my experience it's usually from a merger, a rename, or someone creating a 'new' site instead of reusing an existing one because they couldn't find it. I'd check the audit trail on both sites to see who created the second one and why. Once I understand that, I handle it in two tracks: get the money back or apply it as a credit against the supplier's next invoice, and separately, clean up the supplier master so duplicate bank accounts across sites either get consolidated or get flagged by a PO-plus-amount cross-check going forward.
commonMistakes: Assuming the duplicate invoice check failed as a system defect rather than recognizing it only matches on invoice number.
Fixing the payment without investigating why a second supplier site with a duplicate bank account was created in the first place.
Treating this purely as a recovery/collections problem without addressing the supplier master data gap that allowed it.
Not checking whether the duplicate entry came from manual keying versus an automated import (e.g., OCR) that could reintroduce the issue.
keyPoints: Recognize that Fusion's duplicate invoice check is invoice-number based and will not catch differently numbered duplicates.
Identify the shared remit-to bank account across two supplier sites as the structural root cause.
Trace supplier site creation history to understand why a redundant site exists.
Recover or credit the duplicate payment and reconcile both invoices.
Consolidate supplier sites or add a PO-plus-amount cross-check to prevent recurrence.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the limitation of the invoice-number-based duplicate check
Identifies the duplicate supplier site/bank account as root cause
Addresses both financial recovery and supplier master data remediation
Proposes a concrete preventive control for recurrence

questions.title: AutoInvoice Rejects Batch Over Revenue Rules
questions.prompt: An AR analyst runs AutoInvoice for a software subscription customer and finds 40 of 300 lines rejected with 'Invalid Accounting Rule' even though the transaction source has worked fine for a year. The rejected lines all belong to a new multi-element arrangement product bundle that Sales began invoicing last week, and the lines carry a revenue recognition rule name that doesn't exist in Receivables setup for that transaction type. Describe your diagnostic approach and fix.
questions.modelAnswer: The error 'Invalid Accounting Rule' from AutoInvoice means the interface lines reference a revenue recognition (accounting) rule code that AutoInvoice cannot resolve against Receivables setup for the transaction type involved, not that the transaction source or AutoInvoice program itself is broken. Because only the new multi-element bundle lines fail while the other 260 post cleanly, the candidate should conclude the issue is scoped to new setup, not a regression. The diagnostic sequence is: (1) pull the rejected lines from the AutoInvoice interface exceptions and read the exact rule name/code being passed, (2) check Receivables 'Manage Accounting Rules' to see whether that rule exists at all, is end-dated, or exists under a different exact code/case, (3) confirm the transaction type and transaction class used for the bundle are both enabled for that accounting rule, since a rule can exist but not be assigned to the specific transaction type. The likely root cause is that the new product bundle requires a multi-element revenue allocation rule that was never created or activated for Receivables, even though it may exist in a revenue management tool upstream. The fix is to create or activate the matching accounting rule in Receivables with the correct duration and type (fixed schedule vs. variable), map it to the transaction type, then resubmit only the rejected lines through AutoInvoice rather than reprocessing the whole batch.
questions.professionalAnswer: Whenever I see a partial AutoInvoice rejection where the source has run cleanly for a year, I immediately stop suspecting the interface program and start looking at what changed - and here it's obviously the new bundle, since every rejected line belongs to it. The first thing I'd check is the exact accounting rule code on the rejected interface lines versus what's actually configured in Manage Accounting Rules in Receivables. Nine times out of ten this turns out to be exactly what it sounds like: the upstream system (CPQ, billing, or revenue management) knows about a new revenue recognition rule for the bundle, but nobody ever created that same rule in Receivables, or it exists but isn't enabled for this transaction type. I'd also check case sensitivity and end dates on the rule - small things, but they bite constantly. Once I confirm the rule is missing or misconfigured, I'd work with whoever owns revenue policy to get the duration and schedule type right - is this ratable over 12 months, point-in-time, or tied to a performance obligation - before I create it, because getting that wrong just creates a different revenue problem. After the rule's live and mapped to the transaction type, I resubmit only the 40 rejected lines, not the whole batch, and I'd flag this as a gap in the product-to-billing setup checklist so new bundles get a Receivables review before go-live next time.
commonMistakes: Assuming AutoInvoice itself is malfunctioning and trying to rerun the whole 300-line batch repeatedly without changing configuration.
Overlooking that an accounting rule can exist in Receivables but not be enabled for the specific transaction type used by the new bundle.
Creating a revenue recognition rule without first confirming the correct schedule type (fixed vs. variable, duration) with whoever owns revenue policy.
Resubmitting the entire batch instead of only the rejected lines, risking duplicate processing of the 260 lines that already posted.
keyPoints: Scope the problem correctly: only new-bundle lines fail, pointing to missing setup rather than a program defect.
Inspect the exact accounting rule code on rejected interface lines against Manage Accounting Rules in Receivables.
Check whether the rule exists but isn't enabled/mapped for the specific transaction type.
Coordinate the correct rule duration/schedule type with revenue policy before creating or activating it.
Resubmit only the rejected lines through AutoInvoice after the fix.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly scopes the issue to the new bundle's missing/misconfigured accounting rule
Describes a precise diagnostic path through interface exceptions and Receivables rule setup
Addresses getting the revenue recognition schedule type correct before implementing
Correctly limits remediation to the rejected lines, not the full batch

questions.title: Lockbox Receipts Misapplied Skew AR Aging
questions.prompt: The collections team flags that a customer's AR aging report shows a large balance in the 90+ days bucket even though the customer insists they paid on time via lockbox two months ago. Review shows a lockbox receipt for $42,000 was automatically applied to an unrelated open debit memo instead of the invoice referenced on the remittance, and the correct invoice remains open and now overdue. Walk through how you would identify why AutoLockbox misapplied the cash and how you'd correct it without breaking reconciliation.
questions.modelAnswer: AutoLockbox applies cash based on matching rules against the remittance data in the bank file, typically invoice number first and falling back to other matching criteria (customer, amount) when an exact invoice match fails or is ambiguous. The candidate should recognize that a $42,000 payment landing on an unrelated debit memo instead of the intended invoice indicates either the remittance data didn't carry a clean invoice number (truncated, reformatted, or missing due to a bank file issue) or the amount exactly matched the debit memo and the matching rule's fallback logic grabbed the first candidate it found. Diagnosis should start with the raw lockbox file for that remittance to see exactly what invoice reference, if any, was transmitted, then review the AutoLockbox matching rule set (match by invoice number, then by amount, then by customer) that was active for that receipt class to understand which rule actually fired. Correction must not simply be deleting the receipt, since that breaks the audit trail and bank reconciliation for an already-cleared deposit; instead, the receipt should be unapplied from the debit memo and reapplied to the correct invoice through standard AR cash application, keeping the original receipt number and bank deposit intact so Cash Management reconciliation to the bank statement is unaffected. Finally, the candidate should recommend reviewing or tightening the matching rule priority so amount-only matches require manual review rather than auto-applying when the invoice reference is unreliable.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd check is the raw remittance data that actually came through the lockbox file, not what Fusion shows after the fact, because I want to know whether the invoice number was even transmitted cleanly. Lockbox misapplications are almost always a data quality issue at the bank or the customer's remittance advice - a truncated field, a reformatted invoice number, something that broke the exact match - and then the matching rule fell back to something looser, like amount only, and grabbed the wrong open item that happened to match $42,000. So I'd look at the AutoLockbox matching rule set that was active on that receipt class and figure out exactly which rule fired. Once I know that, fixing the money is the easy part conceptually but needs care: I would never just delete the receipt, because that receipt already cleared the bank and is sitting in a reconciled deposit - deleting it creates a reconciliation break that's worse than the original problem. Instead, I unapply it from the debit memo and reapply it to the correct invoice, keeping the same receipt number and deposit reference so Cash Management reconciliation never has to be touched. Then I'd go back to whoever owns the matching rule configuration and ask whether amount-only matches above a certain dollar threshold should route to manual review instead of auto-applying, because a $42,000 blind match is exactly the kind of exception that should have a human look at it first.
commonMistakes: Deleting or voiding the receipt to 'start over' instead of unapplying and reapplying it, which breaks bank reconciliation for an already-cleared deposit.
Assuming AutoLockbox itself is defective rather than checking the actual remittance data transmitted in the bank file.
Fixing the single misapplied receipt without reviewing the matching rule priority that allowed an amount-only fallback match.
Overlooking that the original intended invoice is now sitting open and overdue and needs its aging status corrected once cash is reapplied.
keyPoints: Identify that AutoLockbox matching rules fell back to a looser match (e.g., amount-only) because the invoice reference in the remittance data was unreliable.
Review the raw lockbox file remittance data, not just the applied result, to find the actual root cause.
Unapply and correctly reapply the receipt rather than deleting it, preserving the bank deposit and reconciliation.
Confirm the correct invoice's aging updates once cash is properly reapplied.
Recommend tightening matching rule priority or thresholds to require manual review on ambiguous matches.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the AutoLockbox matching rule fallback as root cause
Proposes a correction method that preserves bank reconciliation integrity
Confirms resolution of the original invoice's aging/open status
Recommends a preventive control on matching rule configuration

questions.title: Suspense Account Balance After Intercompany Run
questions.prompt: After month-end intercompany processing, the corporate controller notices a non-zero balance sitting in the GL suspense account for the US ledger, which should always net to zero once intercompany balancing completes. The balance appeared after a new intercompany organization was added mid-month, and the amount exactly matches the net of transactions routed through that entity. Explain your root-cause investigation and how you would clear the suspense balance correctly.
questions.modelAnswer: A non-zero intercompany suspense balance means the intercompany balancing engine could not derive a matching due-to/due-from account for at least one leg of a transaction and posted the difference to suspense instead, by design, rather than leaving the journal unbalanced. Since the amount exactly equals the net of transactions through the newly added entity, the candidate should conclude the new organization's intercompany setup is incomplete, most likely missing an intercompany balancing rule (or entry in the intercompany organization/transaction flow setup) that tells the system which receivable/payable account pair to use when this entity trades with other entities in the ledger. The investigation should: (1) identify the specific journal lines that hit suspense and their originating subledger and transaction type, (2) check whether the new entity was added to the intercompany organization definitions and assigned to the correct ledger and legal entity, (3) review the intercompany balancing rules (or legacy intercompany rules) to confirm a rule exists covering this entity-to-entity combination for the relevant transaction type, and (4) confirm the trading partner relationships were set up bidirectionally. Once the missing rule or organization assignment is added, the candidate should reverse the suspense entries for the affected transactions and either rerun intercompany balancing/Create Accounting for those transactions so they post correctly to due-to/due-from accounts, or book a manual correcting journal only as a last resort, and should not close the period until suspense is zero.
questions.professionalAnswer: Suspense account activity in intercompany is never random - it's the system telling me it didn't know where to put the other side of a transaction, so the first thing I'd check is exactly which journal lines landed in suspense and trace them back to their source transactions. Since the dollar amount lines up exactly with the new entity's net activity, I'm not going to waste time looking anywhere else; I go straight to how that entity was set up. Here's exactly how I'd work this: I pull up the intercompany organization definitions and confirm the new entity is actually assigned to the ledger and legal entity correctly, then I check the intercompany balancing rules to see if there's a rule covering transactions between this entity and the others it traded with this month. In my experience, this is almost always a missing rule - someone added the new org for transaction entry but nobody circled back to add the balancing rule before month-end, so the engine had no instruction and defaulted to suspense rather than leaving things unbalanced. Once I add the rule and confirm the trading partner relationship works both directions, I don't just plug a manual entry - I reverse what's in suspense and rerun balancing or Create Accounting on those specific transactions so they post properly to due-to/due-from. And I hold the period open until that suspense balance is genuinely zero, not just offset by something else.
commonMistakes: Booking a manual journal to zero out the suspense account without fixing the underlying intercompany setup gap.
Assuming the suspense balance is a one-time rounding or timing difference rather than tracing it to the specific new entity.
Closing or allowing close of the period while suspense remains non-zero.
Fixing the intercompany balancing rule but not reprocessing the already-posted suspense transactions through balancing/Create Accounting.
keyPoints: Recognize suspense postings as the balancing engine's fallback when it cannot derive a due-to/due-from account pair.
Trace the exact transactions in suspense back to the new intercompany entity.
Check the new entity's intercompany organization assignment and balancing rule coverage, including bidirectional trading partner setup.
Add the missing rule/assignment, then reverse and reprocess the affected transactions rather than booking a manual plug.
Hold the period open until the suspense balance is genuinely zero.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why intercompany suspense balances occur
Traces root cause to the new entity's incomplete intercompany setup
Proposes reprocessing transactions rather than a manual plug
Addresses period-close governance (not closing with non-zero suspense)

questions.title: Create Accounting Fails for New Secondary Ledger
questions.prompt: A finance team stands up a new secondary ledger for statutory reporting in a European subsidiary, and the first week's Create Accounting process ends in 'Error' status for every AP subledger journal, while the primary ledger continues to account fine. The accounting event log shows 'No accounting rule found for Account Rule Type: Supplier Liability' for the new ledger's accounting method. Explain how you would isolate and resolve this configuration gap.
questions.modelAnswer: The error indicates that Subledger Accounting could not find an account rule to derive the supplier liability account for transactions posting under the secondary ledger's accounting method, which is a classic symptom of standing up a new ledger by copying setup incompletely rather than a transaction data problem, since the primary ledger processes identically sourced transactions fine. The candidate should recognize that each ledger can have its own subledger accounting method, and when a new accounting method is created for the secondary ledger (whether copied or built fresh to support different statutory accounting treatment), every component underneath it, journal line rules, account rules, and the mapping set or value sets they reference, must be fully built and attached, not just the header. The diagnosis should: (1) open the secondary ledger's assigned subledger accounting method in Manage Accounting Rules and locate the journal line rule for AP supplier liability, (2) check whether an account rule is attached to that journal line rule at all, or whether it's attached but points to a mapping set/chart of accounts combination that doesn't exist for this ledger's chart of accounts, (3) compare side by side against the primary ledger's working accounting method to find exactly what step was skipped when the new method was created. The fix is to build or correctly attach the missing account rule (typically mapping supplier site or natural account segment values to the correct liability account) for this ledger's chart of accounts, then resubmit Create Accounting for the errored events rather than re-running all AP processing.
questions.professionalAnswer: When Create Accounting fails for every single transaction in a brand-new ledger while the primary ledger keeps working fine, I don't even look at the transactions - I know immediately this is a setup gap in the new accounting method, because real transaction data problems don't fail 100% of the time uniformly like this. The error message is actually doing me a favor here: it's telling me exactly which piece is missing, an account rule for Supplier Liability. So I go straight into Manage Accounting Rules for the secondary ledger's accounting method and look at the journal line rule for the AP liability line - either there's no account rule attached at all, or there's one attached but it references a mapping set built against the wrong chart of accounts. My go-to move at this point is a side-by-side comparison with the primary ledger's accounting method, because whoever stood up the new ledger almost certainly copied some of the setup but missed finishing this one rule, which happens constantly when teams are moving fast to meet a statutory go-live date. Once I find the gap, I build or reattach the correct account rule mapped to this ledger's own chart of accounts values, and then - this part matters - I don't rerun all of AP, I resubmit just the errored accounting events so I'm not reprocessing transactions that have nothing to do with this issue.
commonMistakes: Treating this as a transaction data issue and investigating individual AP invoices instead of the ledger's accounting method setup.
Assuming the new ledger inherited complete setup automatically just because it was copied from or modeled after the primary ledger.
Attaching an account rule that references a mapping set built for the wrong chart of accounts, causing a different downstream error.
Rerunning all AP accounting for the period instead of resubmitting only the errored events once the rule is fixed.
keyPoints: Recognize a 100% failure rate on one ledger as a setup gap in that ledger's accounting method, not a transaction issue.
Locate the specific journal line rule for AP Supplier Liability in the secondary ledger's accounting method.
Determine whether an account rule is missing entirely or attached to the wrong mapping set/chart of accounts.
Compare against the working primary ledger setup to find the exact gap.
Build/correct the account rule for the correct chart of accounts and resubmit only the errored events.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies this as an SLA configuration gap on the new ledger's accounting method
Describes a precise path through journal line rules and account rules to isolate the gap
Proposes comparison against the working primary ledger setup as a diagnostic technique
Correctly scopes the fix to resubmitting only errored events

questions.title: Subledger Entries Transfer With Wrong FX Amounts
questions.prompt: A multinational client's GL team notices that journal entries transferred from the AR subledger for a Mexican entity are posting to GL in USD at amounts that don't match the subledger's functional currency conversion, even though the transfer completed without error. Research shows the ledger's conversion rate type was changed from 'Corporate' to 'Spot' for the current period, but the subledger accounting method still references the old rate type in its journal line rule. Describe how you'd trace and correct this discrepancy.
questions.modelAnswer: The symptom, a clean transfer with no errors but mismatched converted amounts, points away from a processing failure and toward two independent currency configurations having drifted out of sync: the ledger-level default conversion rate type used for period-end reporting changed to 'Spot,' but the subledger accounting method's journal line rule for this entity still has 'Corporate' hard-coded or defaulted as the rate type used when Create Accounting converts the transaction currency amount to ledger currency. Because the transfer and posting succeed technically, no error is raised; the entries simply book at a different rate than the GL team now expects. The diagnostic approach is: (1) confirm the actual rate type used on the posted subledger journal by drilling into the journal source/category and the rate type field on the SLA distribution, (2) compare that against the ledger's currently defined conversion rate type for the period, (3) locate where the rate type is set within the accounting method, whether at the journal line rule, the accounting method options, or an override at the legal entity/ledger assignment level. The fix is to update the subledger accounting method's rate type reference to align with 'Spot' (or whichever rate type is now the standard), reprocess the affected period's transactions through Create Accounting so they re-convert using the correct rate, and reverse/replace the originally posted entries in GL rather than leaving both versions standing, since the subledger is the system of record that must be corrected and retransferred, not adjusted directly in GL.
questions.professionalAnswer: This one's a classic case of two systems of truth drifting apart without anyone getting an error to tell them. No error on the transfer means I'm not looking for a broken process - I'm looking for two currency settings that used to agree and now don't. The first thing I'd check is what rate type is actually stamped on the posted subledger distribution versus what the ledger's current conversion rate type setting says it should be, and here that's immediately obvious once someone tells me the ledger moved to Spot but the accounting method is still wired to Corporate. The part I always explain in interviews is that changing a ledger's rate type doesn't automatically ripple down into every subledger accounting method that references currency conversion - those are separate setups, and whoever made the ledger change probably didn't realize SLA had its own reference to update. Once I confirm that's the gap, I go fix the rate type in the journal line rule for that accounting method so it points to Spot going forward. Then, critically, I don't just leave the already-posted entries as-is or patch them with a GL-level adjustment - the subledger is the source of truth, so I reverse what was transferred, rerun Create Accounting on those transactions so they recalculate at the right rate, and let the corrected version transfer to GL cleanly, so AR and GL agree down to the rate type, not just the total.
commonMistakes: Correcting the mismatched amounts with a manual GL journal adjustment instead of fixing and reprocessing the subledger.
Assuming the transfer process is broken because no one expects a 'successful but wrong' outcome.
Fixing the rate type going forward but leaving the already-posted, incorrectly converted entries uncorrected in both the subledger and GL.
Not checking whether the rate type is set at the journal line rule, the accounting method, or an entity-level override, and fixing the wrong layer.
keyPoints: Recognize that a clean transfer with mismatched amounts points to a currency configuration mismatch, not a processing error.
Identify that the ledger's conversion rate type setting and the subledger accounting method's journal line rule rate type can drift out of sync independently.
Drill into the posted distribution to confirm the actual rate type used versus the ledger's current standard.
Correct the rate type reference in the accounting method's journal line rule.
Reverse and reprocess the affected subledger transactions (not a GL-level plug) so the subledger remains the system of record.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the ledger vs. SLA conversion rate type mismatch
Describes a precise trace through posted distributions and accounting method configuration
Proposes correcting and reprocessing the subledger rather than patching GL directly
Addresses keeping subledger and GL in agreement after correction

questions.title: New Asset Class Depreciates at Wrong Rate
questions.prompt: The fixed-assets accountant reports that a batch of laptops added last quarter under a newly created asset category is showing noticeably less depreciation expense than the same model purchased the prior quarter under an existing category, despite identical cost and life. Review shows the new category was assigned a prorate convention of 'Actual Days' while the depreciation calendar and existing category both use 'Mid-Month'. Explain your diagnostic steps and how you would correct the affected assets.
questions.modelAnswer: The prorate convention determines what fraction of a period's depreciation an asset picks up based on its date placed in service, and a mismatch between the convention assigned to an asset category and the one the rest of the book expects will produce exactly this symptom: identical cost and life assets depreciating at different rates purely because of when the prorate calculation anchors the period fraction. The candidate should identify that 'Actual Days' and 'Mid-Month' calculate the first-period (and sometimes ongoing) depreciation fraction differently, so the new category's assets are being prorated on a different basis than the depreciation calendar's periods are structured for, producing a lower expense in the period examined. Diagnosis should: (1) confirm the prorate convention and prorate date for a sample new-category asset versus the comparable existing-category asset, (2) check the asset category's default prorate convention assignment in Manage Asset Categories, (3) confirm whether the convention mismatch was a setup oversight when the category was created (likely, since the depreciation calendar and every other category use Mid-Month) versus an intentional business decision for this specific asset class. Correction requires more than editing the category going forward, since assets already added under the wrong convention have accumulated depreciation calculated on the wrong basis; the affected assets' prorate convention must be corrected at the asset level (where Fusion Assets permits a convention change, typically before significant depreciation has run, or via an audited correcting adjustment), depreciation must be rolled back and rerun for the affected periods, and the asset category default should be corrected immediately to prevent any further assets from being added incorrectly.
questions.professionalAnswer: Identical cost, identical life, different depreciation expense almost always means something about the calculation basis is different, not the inputs - so I go straight to prorate convention and prorate date before I look at anything else. Here it's basically handed to me: the new category is on Actual Days while everything else, including the depreciation calendar itself, is built around Mid-Month. Those two conventions literally calculate the fraction of the period an asset depreciates for differently, so of course two otherwise-identical laptops come out with different expense. What I want to understand next is whether this was a deliberate decision - maybe someone wanted a different treatment for this asset class - or just an oversight when the category was created, and nine times out of ten when it's this inconsistent with everything else in the book, it's an oversight, probably someone picked a value off a dropdown without realizing the implication. Once I confirm that, the fix has two layers: I correct the asset category default so no more assets get added wrong going forward, and separately I deal with the assets that already exist under the bad convention, which usually means correcting the prorate convention at the asset level and rolling back and rerunning depreciation for the periods affected, with the fixed assets team reviewing the resulting adjustment before it posts. I wouldn't just let it ride and fix it prospectively only - the prior periods are genuinely wrong and need to be corrected, not just the future.
commonMistakes: Assuming the depreciation difference is a rounding or cost basis error instead of checking the prorate convention first.
Fixing only the asset category default going forward without correcting the already-added assets' accumulated depreciation.
Changing the prorate convention on assets that have already run significant depreciation without an audited correcting adjustment.
Not confirming whether the convention mismatch was intentional before treating it purely as a defect.
keyPoints: Identify the prorate convention mismatch (Actual Days vs. Mid-Month) as the direct cause of the depreciation difference.
Confirm the mismatch at the asset category setup level (Manage Asset Categories) against the depreciation calendar's expectation.
Determine whether the mismatch was an oversight or an intentional business decision.
Correct the asset category default to prevent further incorrect additions.
Correct and roll back/rerun depreciation for already-affected assets, not just future additions.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the prorate convention mismatch as root cause
Describes a clear diagnostic comparison between new and existing category setup
Addresses correcting both the category default and already-affected assets
Notes the need for an audited correction rather than a silent change
